quotes.name: Marisio Curazo
quotes.quote: When I see a number like 140 sick in Chinatown, I don't see a number — I see the families I work with every day. Most of them aren't going to the hospital. They're staying home because that's what we do. The daughter takes the bus from Fruitvale to cook. The nephew calls in late to pick up prescriptions. I'm the one who helps figure out who needs a home health aide, who needs their meds delivered, who just needs someone to check in. The hospital has six of our folks right now — the ones who really couldn't stay home. The rest of us are doing what we've always done: taking care of each other, block by block, door by door.

quotes.name: Omarion Farah
quotes.quote: People talk in the cab, but not about hospitals much. They're more worried about who's going to cover a shift or pick up the kids. I see folks staying home, taking care of each other. The ones I hear about going to the hospital are the ones who really can't avoid it. It's a lot of home care, a lot of family stepping in.

quotes.name: Yu Zen
quotes.quote: When I was in that hospital bed after my accident, I kept thinking about the numbers I deal with every day as an insurance broker — the claims, the paperwork, the names on the forms. But lying there, I realized the names on the forms aren't the same as the names on the beds. Chinatown's been hit so hard, and I know it's not because those folks are any less careful or any less strong. It's that when illness clusters, it lands on households where someone's already stretched thin — caring for a parent, watching the grandkids, working two jobs. The six of us in hospital care, we've got nurses and monitors and someone bringing us meals. The other 134 — they've got a cousin or an auntie or a neighbor who's doing all that and still trying to keep the shop open. That's who's caring for them. And that's the part that keeps me up at night, because I know that kind of care doesn't show up on any ledger.
